kobeissi-intel-erases-rally:
Intel's stock erased its entire post-earnings rally within days, wiping out roughly $90 billion in market cap from the rally's peak, Kobeissi reports. Intel had posted 59% growth in its Data Center and AI segment on Tuesday, but still logged an $11 billion GAAP net loss.

## Why did the rally actually reverse
Per Motley Fool's July 24 coverage, Intel shares jumped nearly 13% after hours the day after earnings, then fell 7.89% in Friday's regular session.
What investors were reconsidering, per that report, wasn't Iran, it was questions about foundry customers, AI progress, high capex, and the possibility Intel taps markets for more funding. Seeking Alpha separately pointed to the foundry unit's $2.1 billion operating loss and execution risk. The Iran war was escalating that same week and did raise market-wide risk aversion, but it wasn't cited as the direct cause of Intel's specific reversal.

@@REF@@Stock Market Today, July 24: Intel Reverses Gains on Foundry and AI Spending Concerns (The Motley Fool, 2026-07-24)|https://www.fool.com/investing/2026/07/24/stock-market-today-july-24/

## Is the $11 billion loss really one-time
No. Reporting from the tradesandgains newsletter and XenoSpectrum traces the loss to a $12.529 billion mark-to-market charge on roughly 158.74 million escrow shares Intel owes the US Commerce Department under its August 2025 CHIPS Act equity deal.
Because Intel's stock rose roughly 170% year to date (from about $36.90 to around $100), the value of that obligation ballooned along with it. On an adjusted basis, Intel was profitable.
tradesandgains states plainly that this is not a one-time item, it resets every quarter with the share price. The government's own already-issued 274.6 million shares, meanwhile, gained roughly $21.8 billion in value over the same stretch.

@@CMP@@The card's original framing|The $11 billion loss came from one-time charges, and the real story is the adjusted-basis profit swing.|What's actually going on|The loss is a recurring mark-to-market charge on the government's equity stake that grows as Intel's own stock rises, while the government's shares gained roughly $21.8 billion over the same period.
Whether you read Intel's number as a one-off writedown or a stock-linked accounting mechanic changes what its finances actually look like.

@@REF@@Intel Posts 25% Revenue Growth Yet Reports $11 Billion Net Loss (XenoSpectrum, 2026-07-25)|https://xenospectrum.com/|https://xenospectrum.com/ogp-default.png

## So what's the thing to actually watch
This is the first quarter this escrow mark-to-market showed up prominently, which means it will keep flowing through Intel's GAAP net income every time the stock moves.
Reading Intel's real performance means separating this accounting swing from adjusted earnings and the foundry unit's actual operating losses. Iran soured the market's mood that week, but it wasn't the direct cause of Intel's own reversal.
kobeissi-sp500-iran-war-selloff:
The S&P 500 erased its intraday gains and closed lower as the Iran war escalated, with Intel's rally reversing the same day and the correlation between AI infrastructure stocks and the semiconductor index collapsing to a 4.5-year low, Kobeissi reports.

## Which day is this actually describing
Lining up the underlying reporting by date shows this isn't one day, it's three different ones compressed together.
On Thursday, July 23, the S&P 500 fell 0.9%. Per Yahoo Finance, that was driven by a Houthi attack on Red Sea tankers pushing Brent toward $97-100, capex fears from Wednesday's Alphabet and Tesla earnings, and a bond-yield spike. Intel hadn't reported yet.
On Friday, July 24, the S&P 500 closed little changed, per TheStreet. That's the day Intel's rally actually reversed, and both TheStreet and The Detroit News point mainly to Tesla's 142% capex jump and chip-sector profit-taking, with Iran and tariffs cited only as secondary factors. Oil actually fell 3.5% that day.
It's only on Monday, July 27, that the phrase Kobeissi uses, gains erased and chips falling, actually appears in the record, but Bloomberg and Fortune reported that day's Iran conflict had paused and oil was dropping, with the chip selloff (Nvidia -4.5%, Intel, AMD and Micron down 6-10%) attributed to fading confidence in the AI chip trade itself.

@@REF@@S&P 500, Nasdaq fall as investors eye earnings, Iran risks and tariffs (The Detroit News, 2026-07-24)|https://www.detroitnews.com/story/business/2026/07/24/sp-500-nasdaq-fall-as-investors-eye-earnings-iran-risks-and-tariffs/91035972007/|https://www.detroitnews.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2026/02/03/PDTN/88489525007-getty-images-2255409920.jpg?crop=5162,2903,x0,y264&width=3200&height=1800&format=pjpg&auto=webp

## Does the SOX correlation statistic hold up
No independent report of a 30-day correlation between AI infrastructure stocks and the SOX collapsing toward zero, the lowest in 4.5 years, was found. This appears to be Kobeissi's own proprietary analysis.
The day 145 count is also slightly off. Counting from the February 28 start, July 24 lands closer to day 147.

@@REF@@US stocks catch a bid as oil tumbles with Iran conflict pause (Bloomberg, 2026-07-27)|https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-27/us-stocks-catch-a-bid-as-oil-tumbles-with-iran-conflict-pause

## So what's the thing to actually watch
Compressing a week's worth of separate events into the day Iran shook the market makes for a cleaner story, but the actual sequence was an oil shock, company-specific worries, and profit-taking, playing out across three separate days.
Iran risk was real background noise all week. But before crediting it for any one day's specific drop, it's worth checking what that day's coverage actually cited.
serenity-googl-waymo-uber-split:
Uber and Google's self-driving unit Waymo may be headed for a split, the Financial Times reported, according to investor commentary account Serenity, who says this confirms a view he's held for over a year, that Waymo would eventually turn from partner to rival.

## What does the split actually mean
Reuters, Bloomberg and CNBC, all citing the FT report, describe something more specific: Waymo has told Uber it will launch its own independent app in exactly two cities, Austin and Atlanta, starting January 2028, ending exclusivity there.
That's not a company-wide breakup, it's an exclusivity deal ending in two markets. Under the existing contract, Waymo stays on Uber's platform in those cities through roughly May 2028. The two companies already ended their pilot in Phoenix in late June.
Cited friction points include Waymo's complaints about vehicle cleanliness and routing, Uber's complaints about vehicle unavailability in bad weather, and terms both sides called unsustainable. Waymo still runs its own app independently in 11 metro areas with over 500,000 weekly paid rides, and continues working with Uber elsewhere.

@@REF@@Uber and Waymo to end exclusivity arrangement in Atlanta and Austin (CNBC, 2026-07-24)|https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/24/uber-and-waymo-to-end-exclusivity-arrangement-in-atlanta-and-austin.html|https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/108255725-1769094685480-7VYxj_8U.jpg?v=1769094774&w=1920&h=1080

## Was Uber actually stuck with only Waymo
Serenity argues Uber should have chosen a neutral operator like Avride instead. But Uber already committed up to $375 million to Avride alongside Nebius back in October 2025.
Uber also holds an 11.5% stake in Lucid, 5.82% in WeRide, and works with Pony.ai/Verne, Nuro, Zoox, Wayve-Nissan, May Mobility, Momenta, Baidu's Apollo Go, and Motional, more than a dozen AV partners.
For the road not taken framing to hold, Uber would have had to actually pass on Avride. It didn't. It's already an investor.

@@CMP@@Serenity's reading|Uber made a mistake choosing Waymo from the start, and is now paying for it.|What's actually confirmed|Only a two-city exclusivity deal is ending, and Uber is already an Avride investor working with over a dozen AV companies simultaneously.
Whether to read this report as a clean breakup or a contract adjustment inside an already-diversified portfolio depends on that gap.

@@REF@@Uber, Nebius invest up to $375 million in autonomous vehicle firm Avride (Investing.com, 2025-10-22)|https://www.investing.com/news/company-news/uber-nebius-invest-up-to-375-million-in-autonomous-vehicle-firm-avride-93CH-4301485

## So what's the thing to actually watch
Waymo can currently only reach riders without Uber's app in the 11 metros where it already runs independently. The Austin and Atlanta shift is still two years out.
What actually matters is how fast Waymo's own app expands past those 11 cities, and how quickly Uber turns its dozen-plus AV partnerships into real, scaled service.
kobeissi-datacenter-power-2035:
US data center electricity demand will surge 253% from 2026 levels to 194 gigawatts by 2035, equal to roughly 194 nuclear reactors' worth of power, with data centers' share of total US electricity use rising from about 6% today to 12% by 2030 and 20% by 2035, Kobeissi reports.

## Where does this number come from
The original source is BloombergNEF (BNEF), reported by Bloomberg on July 21. The 194 GW and 20% by 2035 figures match exactly.
But that forecast is itself 83% above BNEF's own previous estimate from December 2025 (106 GW), which was itself a big jump from BNEF's April 2025 estimate of 78 GW. That's three different BNEF numbers in 15 months: 78, then 106, then 194 gigawatts.
No secondary source reports the exact 253% figure verbatim. Tom's Hardware and DataCenterDynamics describe it as 83% above the prior forecast, while TechCrunch calls it four times today's level. Back-calculating from a roughly 55 GW 2026 baseline does get you to 194 divided by 55, or plus 253%, so the arithmetic checks out, but no secondary report states that baseline explicitly.

@@REF@@AI Boom to Drive Data Center Electricity Demand to 20% of US Total by 2035 (Bloomberg, 2026-07-21)|https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-21/data-centers-on-track-to-suck-up-a-fifth-of-us-power-use-by-2035

## What do other research houses say
EPRI puts the 2030 data center share at 9-17%. A World Resources Institute roundup of multiple forecasters shows a range from Lawrence Berkeley National Lab's 6.7-12% up to Boston Consulting Group's roughly 25%.
BNEF's 12% (2030) and 20% (2035) sit toward the upper-middle of that wide range. This is one estimate among several, not a settled consensus.

@@REF@@US data center power demand surpasses 150 GW, with PJM and ERCOT accounting for 60% of the facilities (Enerdatics, 2025-08-04)|https://www.enerdatics.com/insights/us-data-center-power-demand-surpasses-150-gw-with-pjm-and-ercot-accounting-for-60-of-the-facilities|https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/679098606c9b257593953e8d/6890dec13a94c8adb86d430c_PR%201.png

## Is the PJM concentration real
Yes. Of over 150 GW of announced US data center capacity tracked by Enerdatics, PJM holds roughly 45% (67 GW) and ERCOT in Texas about 13% (20 GW). BNEF projects PJM will send 34% of its electricity to data centers by 2035.
Per an Introl blog post from February 2026, PJM's queue for large new interconnections holds over 60 GW pending, with average waits exceeding four years. The national average interconnection wait has grown from under two years in 2008 to about five years now.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
The bigger picture, power replacing chips as the AI buildout's real bottleneck, is already showing up in utility earnings (Southern Company's data-center-driven demand up 42%, Duke Energy with 7.6 GW under contract).
But the precise 2035 number should be read as the latest, most aggressive version of a forecast that's more than doubled in 15 months, not a fixed target.
trump-eu-301-investigation-bigtech-fines:
President Trump announced a Section 301 investigation into what he calls the EU robbing American companies through antitrust fines, citing $15 billion against Apple, $3 billion against Meta, $2.5 billion against Amazon, and a new $1 billion against Google, for a claimed cumulative total above $18 billion, and threatened a substantial tariff in response.

## Starting with Apple's $15 billion
The actual EU antitrust and Digital Markets Act fine against Apple in 2025-2026 was 500 million euros, about $571 million, issued in April 2025 over App Store anti-steering restrictions.
The $15 billion figure is actually the 2016 EU ruling ordering Ireland to recover roughly 13.1 billion euros plus interest in back taxes from Apple. That ruling was upheld by the EU's top court in September 2024, and Ireland withdrew about 14.25 billion euros, roughly $15.5 billion, from escrow in 2025. It's a tax case from 2016, not an antitrust fine, and 9to5Mac fact-checked this exact conflation in Trump's own post.

@@REF@@Trump vows retaliation over EU fines against Apple and other great US tech giants (9to5Mac, 2026-07-24)|https://9to5mac.com/2026/07/24/trump-vows-retaliation-over-eu-fines-against-apple-and-other-great-us-tech-giants/|https://i0.wp.com/9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2025/04/tim-cook-trump.jpg?resize=1200%2C628&quality=82&strip=all&ssl=1

## What about Meta and Amazon
Meta's actual DMA fine was 200 million euros, about $220 million, issued in April 2025 over its pay or consent ad model. No fine matching $3 billion was found, roughly a 15x overstatement.
No matching EU antitrust or DMA fine against Amazon was found at all. Amazon's actual live EU regulatory issue is a preliminary gatekeeper designation for AWS cloud services from June 2026, not a fine.

@@REF@@EU fines Meta and Apple under Digital Markets Act (NPR, 2025-04-23)|https://www.npr.org/2025/04/23/nx-s1-5373560/apple-meta-eu-tech-fines

## Did Google really just get fined $1 billion
That part checks out. The EU fined Google 890 million euros, about $1 billion, on July 23 over Search and Play Store DMA breaches. But cumulative above $18 billion doesn't hold up precisely.
Confirmed prior Google EU fines add up to roughly $13-15 billion: the 2017 Shopping case (2.42B euros), 2018 Android case (4.1-4.34B euros, upheld on appeal July 2, 2026), 2019 AdSense case (1.49B euros), and a September 2025 adtech fine (roughly $3.45B). That doesn't clearly clear $18 billion.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
Section 301 really is the same legal tool Trump used to launch tariffs against China. But he's also threatened the EU with 50% and 100% tariffs before without following through.
Three of the four dollar figures behind this threat don't check out or are inflated, and only Google's new fine is accurate. Whether that shaky foundation still ends in real tariffs, or another walked-back threat, is a separate question worth watching regardless.
jensen-open-models-letter:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang posted on X for the first time on July 24, using it to share a letter titled Open Weights and American AI Leadership, arguing open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity and protect national AI sovereignty.

## Who actually signed
Per Fortune and Tom's Hardware, the letter launched with roughly 25 signers, Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, Palantir, Hugging Face, IBM, Mistral, Dell, and a16z among them. OpenAI and Google weren't on it.
Forbes reported the signer list roughly doubled to about 50 within a day, as OpenAI, Google, AMD, Cisco and GitHub joined late. Anthropic and Amazon never signed at all.

@@REF@@Jensen Huang just used his first ever X post to warn the AI industry not to make the mistake that software narrowly avoided in the 1980s (Fortune, 2026-07-24)|https://fortune.com/2026/07/24/jensen-huang-open-source-letter-nvidia-kimi/|https://fortune.com/img-assets/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/GettyImages-2286326398-e1784913912763.jpg?resize=1200,600

## Why did Anthropic sit this out
Per Axios, July 27, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei declined to join, citing a safety concern that open-weight models cannot be recalled once released.
That's a substantive safety objection, not just competitive positioning. The timing is notable too. Four days earlier, reports surfaced that the White House was reviving a push to restrict Chinese open-weight models, including Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, released July 16, accused of distilling US models, and days after Xi Jinping made his own openness pitch at China's World AI Conference on July 17, announcing a rival body, the World AI Cooperation Organization, with 29 countries signed on.

@@REF@@Big Tech lines up in support of open-weight AI (Axios, 2026-07-27)|https://www.axios.com/2026/07/27/nvidia-anthropic-openai-open-weight-debate|https://images.axios.com/T0kiLOXo8ikXMd6Vj1NWbBlEfHQ=/0x0:1920x1080/1366x768/2026/03/26/1774548278869.jpeg

## Why is Nvidia the one pushing this
Per Yahoo Finance, Nvidia controls roughly 81% of the data-center AI chip market, and more open models spreads chip demand across many more buyers instead of concentrating it in a few efficiency-optimizing closed API providers, a commercial interest baked into the position.
Huang himself is quoted saying more AI use means you'll have to sell more Nvidia computers. Forbes summed it up as every signatory argues for openness in someone else's yard. Nvidia itself owns proprietary CUDA and is a $26 billion investor in OpenAI.

## So what's the thing to actually watch
Whether to read this letter as industry-wide consensus or a coalition that joined at different times for different self-interested reasons comes down to who signed when, and who didn't.
What actually matters is whether this shapes Washington's real export and procurement rules, and how the signatories answer the cannot be recalled safety concern Anthropic raised by staying out.
kobeissi-ai-capex-sox-correlation-collap:
The stock market is starting to treat AI chipmakers and AI spenders as two separate trades instead of one. The 30-day correlation between the largest US AI-infrastructure spenders and the semiconductor index, the SOX, has fallen to near zero, the lowest reading in at least four and a half years, down from +0.78 in April and well below the +0.60 average since 2022.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/BalticServers_data_center.jpg/960px-BalticServers_data_center.jpg|Inside a data center like this, GPUs and storage live together. This is exactly what hyperscalers are building.|BalticServers.com · CC BY-SA 3.0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:BalticServers_data_center.jpg

## The stat traces to Charles Schwab, not Kobeissi
The Kobeissi Letter presented this correlation collapse as its own read, but the underlying chart comes from Kevin Gordon, senior investment strategist at Charles Schwab.

@@REF@@Big Tech's Trillion-Dollar Bet Is Starting to Crack, Investors Are Looking Elsewhere for Profits (24/7 Wall St., 2026-07-25)|https://247wallst.com/investing/2026/07/25/big-techs-trillion-dollar-bet-is-starting-to-crack-investors-are-looking-elsewhere-for-profits/|https://247wallst.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/shutterstock-2122253927-huge-licensed-scaled.jpg

That piece cites Gordon's research and confirms the same figures, though Gordon's original tweet or chart couldn't be independently verified beyond this outlet's citation.

## Since early June, the two groups have moved apart
Semiconductor stocks have rallied even as the hyperscalers pouring hundreds of billions into data centers have declined, and the pattern has run in reverse on other days too. Chipmakers keep benefiting from AI demand regardless of who is paying for it, while hyperscalers face growing questions about whether their spending will generate enough revenue to justify the cost.

## Is fading chip demand really the cause
Commerzbank offers a different explanation. It isn't that chip demand cooled, the bank argues, but that hyperscalers' cash-flow erosion and rising debt loads are the real story behind the split.

@@REF@@Equities: Hyperscaler stress and chip volatility (Commerzbank via FXStreet, 2026-07-24)|https://www.fxstreet.com/news/equities-hyperscaler-stress-and-chip-volatility-commerzbank-202607241704|https://editorial.fxsstatic.com/images/i/General-Stocks_2_Medium.png

The note points out that all but one of the top five hyperscalers now have five-year credit default swaps trading above the investment-grade index, meaning credit risk, not chip demand, is what's cracking first.

@@CMP@@Demand-cooling case|Chip demand itself is fading, splitting chipmaker and spender stocks apart|Balance-sheet-stress case|Chip demand hasn't changed, but hyperscaler cash flow and debt are cracking first

## So what decides the next phase
A falling correlation means chipmakers can keep winning even if a hyperscaler's spending disappoints, but it also means the market is starting to grade AI spenders on returns, not just on how much they spend. Watch whether hyperscaler cash flow and credit metrics improve next earnings season, or whether the stress Commerzbank flags widens, to tell whether this crack is temporary or structural.
netinterest-stripe-paypal-bid:
Stripe and private equity firm Advent first surfaced as bidders for PayPal in a Reuters exclusive on July 15. The offer values PayPal at roughly $53 billion, $60.50 a share, with Stripe and Advent each taking half the combined entity, backed by about $50 billion in bank financing arranged by JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley, with roughly $17 billion coming from Stripe and Advent's own equity.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/NY_stock_exchange_traders_floor_LC-U9-10548-6.jpg/960px-NY_stock_exchange_traders_floor_LC-U9-10548-6.jpg|A US exchange floor. PayPal shares jumped the day this offer broke.|Thomas J. O'Halloran · Public domain|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:NY_stock_exchange_traders_floor_LC-U9-10548-6.jpg

@@REF@@Stripe, Advent make $53 billion takeover offer for PayPal, sending stock soaring (CNBC/Reuters, 2026-07-15)|https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/15/stripe-advent-offer-to-buy-paypal-for-more-than-53-billion-reuters.html|https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/108300726-1777652911172-gettyimages-2262985849-boivin-notitle260225_npaSd.jpeg?v=1777652966&w=1920&h=1080

## The board called it inadequate, not a rejection
Net Interest's Marc Rubinstein wrote about this deal on July 24. But a day after the original report, Reuters had already broken that PayPal's board views the offer as inadequate and is working with Goldman Sachs and Evercore on a response. That's as far as tier-one reporting goes: no formal rejection, no confirmed counter-price.

@@REF@@Exclusive: PayPal board sees Stripe-Advent offer as inadequate, sources say (Reuters via Yahoo Finance, 2026-07-16)|https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/articles/exclusive-paypal-board-sees-stripe-222532613.html|https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/A0E0171A569EA924D744E2CE1B067B46A82D6D46E7BC407762D073A7EE441305/subgraphmysterio/resizefill_w1200_h800;quality_80;format_webp/https:%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Freuters-finance.com%2Fc0b9d29dfa1bb0040e2518ba0985bf08

## Where does the $70-a-share figure come from
Several outlets since have reported PayPal "rejected" the bid and wants closer to $70 a share. Tracing that back, it lands closer to analyst speculation, including from William Blair's Andrew Jeffrey, than to anything Reuters, Bloomberg or CNBC has confirmed.

@@CMP@@Tier-one reporting|Confirms only that the board finds the offer inadequate and is weighing a response with advisors|Secondary reporting|Goes further, to a formal rejection and a $70-a-share counter, but traces to analyst estimates rather than confirmed sourcing

## The debt from 2013, and a reversed scorecard
The bid closes a loop dating to 2013, when eBay-owned PayPal tried to buy Stripe outright and was turned down by founders Patrick and John Collison, buying Braintree, maker of Venmo, for $800 million instead. Over the following decade, Stripe's payment volume compounded at 70% a year to $1.9 trillion last year, while Braintree grew 43% a year to $600 billion.

## So where does this deal actually stand
Two things are solid: Stripe won that old rivalry decisively, and PayPal's board currently calls the price too low. Whether the deal closes, and at what price, is still open, and the next real signal will be PayPal's board issuing a formal position or Stripe raising its offer.
kobeissi-oracle-cds-record: Oracle's cost of insuring against a default has hit a record, with five-year credit default swaps trading near 203 basis points, meaning investors now pay roughly $203,000 a year to insure $10 million of the company's debt against non-payment, The Kobeissi Letter reports. That level has more than quadrupled since mid-2025 and now sits above where Oracle's CDS traded at the peak of the 2008 financial crisis. The stress shows up in the bond market too. Oracle's 6.7% notes due 2056 widened 8 basis points this week to a 263 basis point spread over Treasurys, and its 5.7% notes due 2036 widened 9 basis points to 205. S&P Global Ratings downgraded Oracle to BBB-, one notch above junk, on July 9th, citing the company's fast-growing spending on AI data centers. Oracle has taken on debt at an unusual pace to build out cloud capacity for AI customers including OpenAI, and investors are increasingly pricing in the risk that revenue from those contracts doesn't arrive fast enough to cover the bill. A further downgrade to junk status would raise Oracle's borrowing costs even more and could trigger selling by funds that only hold investment-grade debt.
jukan-samsung-hynix-silicon-valley-deal:
Ahead of President Lee Jae-myung's Silicon Valley trip, presidential chief of staff for policy Kim Yong-beom previewed 'very large-scale' supply contracts for Samsung Electronics and SK hynix with major US tech firms, without naming which companies or whether the deals covered memory, foundry work, or both.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Tesla-NVIDIA_GPU_cluster_%283706444821%29.jpg/960px-Tesla-NVIDIA_GPU_cluster_%283706444821%29.jpg|A cluster built from many GPUs stacked together, the kind of infrastructure these AI deals are meant to feed.|ChrisDag · CC BY 2.0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tesla-NVIDIA_GPU_cluster_(3706444821).jpg

## The vague preview turned into hard numbers within days
On July 25, what actually got announced was far more specific than the preview. Samsung signed a roughly $200 billion, five-year deal (through 2030) with Broadcom covering HBM supply for AI accelerators, sub-2nm foundry production and advanced packaging.

@@REF@@Samsung wins $200 billion order to supply chips to Broadcom (Fortune, 2026-07-25)|https://fortune.com/2026/07/25/samsung-200-billion-order-supply-2-nanometer-chips-broadcom/|https://fortune.com/img-assets/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/GettyImages-2284413802-e1785010814998.jpg?resize=1200,600

## SK hynix's side involved both Nvidia and Microsoft
SK Group signed a roughly $500 billion letter of intent with Nvidia covering multi-gigawatt AI data-center buildout and long-term HBM supply, and separately reportedly extended HBM4 supply to Microsoft. SK's combined big-tech partnerships were put at roughly $750 billion over five years.

@@REF@@NVIDIA Secures SK Hynix HBM Memory In $500B AI Infrastructure Deal (HotHardware, 2026-07-25)|https://hothardware.com/news/nvidia-secures-sk-hynix-hbm-memory-500b-ai-infrastructure-deal|https://hothardware.com/contentimages/NewsItem/71209/content/16x9_2133x1200_highres-nvidia-sign.jpg

Worth flagging: the roughly $250 billion figure attributed to Microsoft is derived by subtracting Nvidia's $500 billion from SK's $750 billion total in one syndicated report, not a standalone confirmed number.

## The presidential office confirmed the total itself
At the San Francisco AI Summit, Kim Yong-beom said Korean firms and US big tech agreed to roughly $950 billion in semiconductor cooperation, pointing directly to the Samsung-Broadcom and SK hynix-Nvidia deals as the substance of his earlier preview. The Korea Herald report carrying those remarks describes the Samsung-Broadcom agreement as a $200 billion memorandum of understanding and folds SK's side into a single $750 billion figure covering Nvidia and other global tech firms, so the $500 billion Nvidia-only breakout above does not appear in that article.

@@REF@@Korea, US tech giants set sights on $950 billion in chip partnerships: Seoul (The Korea Herald, 2026-07-25)|https://www.koreaherald.com/article/10819973|https://wimg.heraldcorp.com/news/cms/2026/07/25/news-p.v1.20260725.a5b80da090f14900a17fe9e42ce7e871_T1.jpg

## What this preview actually left behind
It's unusual for commercial contracts normally negotiated privately between companies to land on numbers that match a presidential-level preview this closely. The thing to watch now is whether Samsung keeps expanding beyond Nvidia and Broadcom, and whether the Microsoft figure gets an independent confirmation of its own.

jukan-morgan-stanley-bearish-memory:
A Morgan Stanley research note turning bearish on memory chips is real and has been circulating among investors, semiconductor analyst Jukan reports after confirming it with his own sources, and Korean financial media have tied it to a sharp KOSPI selloff.

The note is credited to Shawn Kim, Morgan Stanley's Asia-Pacific technology research head, who has made bearish semiconductor calls before. He argues NAND flash makers are holding roughly 13 weeks of unsold inventory, near the roughly 15-week peak seen during Covid, and that demand has evaporated. ## Why buyers are pulling back
Big cloud companies say their own chip inventories are already healthy. Tencent has reportedly locked in 90% of what it needs, and China's CXMT is ramping supply fast, all pulling supply and demand back into balance. NAND spot prices have been falling for two months. The note extends the same logic to DRAM and caps HBM growth near 40%, citing TrendForce data.

## It's not public, and it's already moving Korean stocks
The note itself hasn't been published anywhere Jukan or Korean outlets could point to directly, all of the corroboration comes from secondary financial press repeating its figures. Even so, Korean coverage reports a single-day KOSPI plunge sharp enough to trigger a circuit breaker around the time the note circulated, with SK hynix and Samsung Electronics both falling more than 8%, alongside other pressures like oil prices and CXMT's blockbuster IPO diverting capital.

The bear case rests on inventory and pricing figures that could shift again within a quarter, while bulls point to structural AI demand this note doesn't fully capture. meru-forced-labor-tariff-korea:
Starting July 24, the United States began applying a 12.5% forced-labor tariff on Korean goods, replacing the 10% global tariff that had been in place, Korean investment blogger Meru writes, meaning Korea's overall tariff burden went up, not down.

## How a Supreme Court ruling led here
The backstory checks out against US trade officials' own account: in February, the Supreme Court ruled the Trump administration's reciprocal (IEEPA) tariffs illegal, so the White House invoked Trade Act Section 122 to impose a temporary 10% global tariff, capped at 150 days and set to expire July 24. Its replacement ties tariffs to whether a country bans imports made with forced labor. The US Trade Representative's own fact sheet confirms the mechanism: Washington reviewed 60 economies covering the large majority of US imports, and found most of them, including Korea, either have no such import ban or don't enforce one.

@@REF@@Fact Sheet: USTR Section 301 Action in Response to the Failure of 60 Economies to Ban Imports Produced with Forced Labor (USTR, 2026-07)|https://ustr.gov/about/policy-offices/press-office/fact-sheets/2026/july/fact-sheet-ustr-section-301-action-response-failure-60-economies-ban-imports-produced-forced-labor|https://ustr.gov/sites/default/files/2026-07/Meta%20Tag_22.png

## Why Korea's rate landed at 12.5%
The rate combines each country's existing most-favored-nation (MFN) tariff with the new levy, capped at 12.5% combined, so goods with 0% MFN like cosmetics take the full add-on, while goods already above that threshold get none. Korea's combined rate came out to 12.5%, confirmed by multiple outlets covering the rollout.

@@REF@@U.S. restores tariffs, caps South Korean goods at 12.5% (UPI, 2026-07-24)|https://www.upi.com/Top_News/World-News/2026/07/24/us-tariffs-section-301/7451784928868/|https://cdnph.upi.com/sv/ph/og/upi/7451784928868/2026/1/b7bbdf482a195655d3bb9b4ab98fc5c4/v1.5/US-restores-tariffs-caps-South-Korean-goods-at-125.jpg

## Meru's math on who got a better deal
Meru reports that Switzerland, Taiwan, and the EU negotiated extra country-specific exemptions, while Korea and Japan did not make that list, a specific claim from his own sourcing that this outlet could not independently verify against USTR's country-by-country list. Semiconductors remain tariff-free under a separate US-Korea agreement, which is more broadly corroborated elsewhere.

## What it costs, by Meru's estimate
Citing the Atlantic Council, Meru estimates this adds roughly $4.3 billion a year in new tariffs on Korean imports, a figure this outlet also could not independently trace to a specific Atlantic Council publication. With no clear countermeasure in sight, Meru argues coordinating with Japan, which faces the same situation, looks like the most realistic option.

## A relabeled tariff, or a real new cost
Korea could shave 2.5 percentage points off this tariff by adopting its own forced-labor import ban, but doing so would invite deeper US scrutiny into supply chains with Xinjiang ties. Whether that trade-off is worth a modest rate cut, against a policy that Meru's own numbers suggest already costs Korean exporters billions a year, is the question Seoul now has to weigh.
meru-saudi-tanker-strike-fallout:
Yemen's Houthi forces claimed strikes on two Saudi-linked oil tankers, the Korean investment blogger Meru writes, days after warning global shipping firms that any vessel touching Saudi ports would be a target.

## What's confirmed and what isn't
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claimed the July 22 strikes on the product tanker Encelia and the VLCC Layla. The Encelia incident is the better-corroborated of the two, with a UKMTO (United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations) notification and a visible fire reported. The Layla strike is Houthi-claimed but has not been independently confirmed by outside reporting. Bahri, Saudi Arabia's state shipping line majority owned by the sovereign wealth fund and Aramco, is confirmed as Layla's owner; Encelia's ownership was not independently verified in available reporting.

@@REF@@Yemen's Houthis claim attack on two Saudi oil tankers (Al Jazeera, 2026-07-22)|https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/7/22/yemens-houthis-claim-attack-on-two-saudi-oil-tankers|https://www.aljazeera.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/ap_6a613e7ed9b96-1784757886.jpg?resize=1920%2C1440

## The warning came first
On July 20, the Houthis told global shipping firms by email that they would treat any vessel loading or unloading cargo at Saudi ports as fair game, regardless of flag. Foreign tankers are not waiting to find out if the threat extends to them. The Houthis themselves claimed nearly ten ships have turned back, a figure that could not be independently corroborated through a specific vessel count as this card originally suggested. EU Naval Force Aspides has advised vessels linked to Israeli, US, or Saudi interests to avoid the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden until threat levels ease.

@@REF@@EU Warns Israeli- and U.S.-Linked Ships to Avoid Red Sea Amid Houthi Saudi Embargo (gCaptain, 2026)|https://gcaptain.com/eu-warns-israeli-and-u-s-linked-ships-to-avoid-red-sea-amid-houthi-saudi-embargo/|https://gcaptain.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/2024-08-26T084011Z_1381620125_RC2KN9AMGEC8_RTRMADP_3_ISRAEL-PALESTINIANS-SHIPPING-YEMEN.jpg

## A geography that has frustrated past US strikes
Meru points out the Houthis hold a geographic advantage that has frustrated past US military action: mountainous terrain riddled with tunnels and bunkers that a 52-day American bombing campaign in 2025, Operation Rough Rider, could not fully destroy despite striking more than 1,000 targets over March 15 to May 6.

## The quieter cost is already showing up
War-risk insurance premiums on Red Sea and Gulf of Aden voyages have already been rising since the attacks, and shipping-trade coverage points to Red Sea transit volumes falling to multi-month lows. That is Meru's core point: the delivered cost of Middle East crude climbs quietly through insurance and rerouting well before any single blockade escalation makes headlines of its own.
kobeissi-us-home-price-record:
US existing-home statistics had two different sources tangled together. NAR's June existing-home sales report, released July 9, put the median sale price at $440,600, up 1.8% year over year, with sales at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.09 million, down 2.4% from May and up 2.8% year over year.

@@REF@@NAR Existing-Home Sales Report Shows 2.4% Decrease in June (National Association of Realtors, 2026-07-09)|https://www.nar.realtor/newsroom/nar-existing-home-sales-report-shows-2-4-decrease-in-june|https://cms.nar.realtor/sites/default/files/2025-11/residential-neighborhood-homes-GettyImages-2148764462-1200w-628h.jpg

## The metro-level surge numbers came from a different company
The claim that San Francisco led with a 9.2% year-over-year gain, followed by Pittsburgh at 9.1% and West Palm Beach at 8.6%, and that new listings fell 0.8% from May to 376,762, the lowest since December, all trace to brokerage Redfin's June report, not NAR.

@@REF@@Redfin Reports U.S. Home Prices Hit All-Time High, Driven in Part By Big Upticks in San Francisco and West Palm Beach (Redfin, 2026-07-13)|https://www.redfin.com/news/home-prices-record-high-june-2026/|https://www.redfin.com/news/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/pexels-jay-lockyer-2674837-28999250-scaled.jpg

The two firms sample and count differently: NAR reports closed, nationwide transactions, while Redfin publishes real-time, brokerage-based metro data.

## Correcting the numbers changes the picture
The impression that national sales hit a four-year high doesn't hold up. By NAR's own numbers, sales actually fell 2.4% month over month. The record price itself, and Redfin's metro-level heat and shrinking listings, are each accurate on their own terms.

## So how should this housing market actually be read
Record prices and shrinking listings are both real, but national sales aren't accelerating. If anything, the more accurate picture is a national market cooling slightly month over month while a handful of hot metros overheat. That distinction matters for how the Fed reads housing's role in inflation and affordability.

There's no rigorous published analysis confirming Indeed data reliably leads official JOLTS figures, and this instance runs counter to the claim. While Indeed postings were falling, the most recent confirmed BLS reading was rising.

The Indeed numbers are real data, but treating them as proof that official statistics will soon weaken is a forecast about figures that don't exist yet. kobeissi-jgb-institutional-demand:
Japanese insurance companies bought $3.9 billion of long-term Japanese government bonds (JGBs, those maturing in 10 years or more) in June, their largest monthly purchase in three years, market commentary account The Kobeissi Letter reports.

## A sharp reversal from May
That's a reversal from May, when insurers were net sellers to the tune of $1.2 billion, and it marks only the second month in the past 11 that insurers have been net buyers of long-term JGBs, according to Kobeissi's figures. Bloomberg independently ran a headline confirming Japanese insurers bought the most super-long bonds in three years in June, corroborating the broad direction of the claim, though the underlying article is paywalled and the specific $3.9 billion and $1.2 billion figures trace to Kobeissi's own data rather than something this outlet could verify line by line.

@@REF@@Japan Insurers Buy Most Super-Long Bonds in Three Years in June (Bloomberg, 2026-07-21)|https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-07-21/japan-insurers-buy-most-super-long-bonds-in-three-years-in-june

## Why insurers matter so much here
Insurers are one of the largest domestic holders of long-dated Japanese debt, so their return as buyers could meaningfully support a bond market that's struggled with weak demand this year, a dynamic that has pushed Japanese yields higher and drawn comparisons to rising Treasury yields elsewhere.

## Tokyo is also pulling other levers
The shift comes as Japanese authorities try to engineer more domestic demand for their own bonds. Japan's finance ministry has floated letting individuals hold JGBs inside a tax-free investment account, and separately, Goldman Sachs estimates Japan's public pension fund GPIF has roughly $75 billion of room to raise its allocation to Japanese assets.

## One good month, or a real turn
This is the second buying month in eleven, not yet a confirmed trend, and it followed direct government encouragement rather than a clearly market-driven shift in appetite. Whether Japanese institutions are actually coming back to their own bond market, or this was a one-off month that reverses once the policy nudges fade, will show up in whether insurers post a third straight month of buying when July's data lands.

jukan-nvidia-800v-hvdc-delay:
Nvidia's next-generation 800 volt HVDC power system, a way of delivering electricity inside AI server racks that cuts energy loss and lets racks scale to higher power levels, may not reach large-scale production until 2028 or later, a year later than the 2027 timeline the market had expected, according to research firm SemiAnalysis.

## Why power, not chip speed, is the bottleneck now
HVDC, short for high-voltage direct current, replaces the many small power converters inside a server rack with fewer, more efficient ones. That matters because AI racks are increasingly limited by how much power and cooling they can pack in, not by chip performance.

@@IMG@@https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Datacenter_Server_Racks_%2822370909788%29.jpg/960px-Datacenter_Server_Racks_%2822370909788%29.jpg|This is the kind of rack infrastructure the 800V HVDC system is meant to power.|Carl Lender · CC BY 2.0|https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Datacenter_Server_Racks_(22370909788).jpg

## Two different reads on the same delay
SemiAnalysis's own reporting has pointed to hyperscalers favoring a more mature low-voltage transition over immediate 800V adoption, alongside related delays in co-packaged optics for Nvidia's Rubin Ultra platform, as part of the story. Semiconductor analyst Jukan, citing supply chain sources, argues the market has misread the delay differently: the issue is a validation problem with first-generation product designs, not a change to Nvidia's technology roadmap. Power cabinets, battery backup units, and battery packs have all been resubmitted for validation testing, these sources say, a normal part of qualifying new hardware.

@@CMP@@SemiAnalysis's read|Hyperscalers are holding back on 800V adoption itself, alongside related packaging delays, pushing the real ramp to 2028|Jukan's supply-chain sources|The roadmap hasn't changed. First-gen hardware just needs to be revalidated, and volume production is still coming in 1Q 2027

## Delta Electronics is said to be ready
Taiwan's Delta Electronics, a major supplier of data center power systems, battery backup units, and energy-management platforms for this architecture, is described as positioned for a ramp once validation clears.

@@REF@@NVIDIA, Google Among First 800V HVDC Adopters (TrendForce, 2026-06-15)|https://www.trendforce.com/news/2026/06/15/news-nvidia-google-may-be-first-to-adopt-800v-hvdc-initial-3q26-shipments-may-boost-delta-and-infrastructure-suppliers/|https://img.trendforce.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/15144210/NVIDIA-800V-HVDC-20260615-624x351.jpg

## What's actually riding on this
The system is meant to support Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin chip platform, and any slip in power hardware readiness could delay how fast data centers can deploy Rubin at scale, even if the chips themselves ship on time. Whether the real culprit is hyperscaler caution or first-gen validation delays matters less to data center operators than the bottom line: how much power they can actually plug in, and when.
